findings.passage: Second, under the worst pain of his life, what he protected was motion. He says he wasn't a good student, so it was not a record. He calls it momentum.
findings.problem: The grief beat is shared 7/3 ground, yet the hook, the type answer and both type FAQs treat it as Seven-discriminating ('the reason starts with that Monday'; 'when grief has hit him, he has sped up instead of stopping'; 'under grief he protected momentum rather than an image'). The rejected Three prediction is a strawman: nobody expects a grieving Three to protect 'a record' or 'an image' at a funeral. The textbook Three defense is shelving feeling to keep doing and finish, which is what he describes. In the Death, Sex & Money passage the draft quotes (S07, about 13:18-15:05, machine transcript), his own causal account runs through his father's achievement refrain, which the draft omits: 'It was always like, that's great. Keep going. You know, it was always like one up yourself or don't stop. And so that's what I did. Like that's how I coped is by, you know, I took more credits than ever.' He threw himself into 'the experience of school in order to finish'; 'I wasn't a good student' corrects 'schoolwork', not striving. The 2020 summer ('I lost myself to the cause') is immersion in a cause, which neither type specifically predicts.
findings.acceptance_test: Either (a) 'Why not Type 3?' labels the Monday and the 2020 summer as shared ground and drops them from the reasons Seven wins, and the type answer, both type FAQs and the hook's 'the reason starts with that Monday' stop presenting them as discriminating; or (b) the article states the Three grief prediction accurately (feeling deferred to keep performing toward a goal), quotes his 'one up yourself or don't stop... that's how I coped' framing, and shows a sourced element of his response that the Three prediction does not cover. 'It was not a record' does not survive either path.

findings.passage: Third, a Three tends to edit failure out of the story. Rahma leaves it in.
findings.problem: This tests a stereotype, and the record answers it the other way. The quoted failures come from the August 2024 newsletter that also announces 'I have checked off all the boxes on the plan'. Failure told from the far side of success is the standard comeback arc, and Threes tell it readily. The 'cringe' resolve (Interview, May 2026, recalled years later) is itself about overriding embarrassment ('I'm not going to be embarrassed'), which is shame management. A year into comedy he was still agonizing over 'comedian' in his bio (the draft's own 'You shouldn't be aspiring. You have to be.'). The opened Forbes interview also contains failure avoidance that the draft omits. When the first Keep the Meter Running episode went up: 'I turned my phone off cuz I was like, I can't deal with another failure. Literally, I was like, I don't want to watch it... I don't want to watch it flop' (S08 auto-captions, about 00:40:02-00:40:35; machine text, speaker by continuity). He adds that he knew it was a hit when a bodega worker recognized him.
findings.acceptance_test: The third reason is cut or recast as shared ground. If any version stays, the same section quotes the phone-off line and the bio agonizing and explains, with a source, why retrospective failure-telling by a creator whose brand is candor separates Seven from Three. 'So why Seven? Three things tip it.' is renumbered to match the reasons that survive.

findings.passage: The thinking part shows quickly in Rahma. Rolling Stone's CT Jones found him hard to interview because he kept turning her questions back on her
findings.problem: The type section introduces the centers ('anger, shame or fear') and then never applies them to the actual contest. Seven is a fear type and Three a shame type, so the center is the cleanest cross-check available, and it goes unused. The only fear-center evidence offered is one interviewer's experience of him turning questions back, which the privacy he describes also explains ('The sunglasses are a disguise... I'm preserving a piece of myself'). Shame/acceptance language in the opened record is plentiful, and some of it is omitted: 'I need to learn how to be a person that people like' (S21); 'accepted into the centers of attention. So I didn't want to say anything weird, do anything weird' (S07); 'trying to figure out my identity as quickly as possible and become that new identity' (Brooklyn Magazine 2023, omitted); press validation as 'manifesting a reality because you're not saying you're a comedian. The headline says you're a comedian' (S08, the omitted lead-in to 'Personally, I do'); 'I'm not going to be embarrassed.' The real fear/deprivation evidence is either filed as an anomaly ('He is careful with money in ways the impulsive Seven of stereotype is not'; 'If it doesn't work out, I can always sell this stuff') or never identified as fear: dread of 'sending emails for a living until I was 80' (S07), 'I think I'll die', 'if I take a semester off to grieve, there's a chance that I won't come back'. Separately, 'A Five barely notices it' misdescribes Fives, who are usually described as pulling back into the mind to manage fear, not as failing to notice it.
findings.acceptance_test: The type section or 'Why not Type 3?' runs the center test. At least two sourced shame/acceptance passages are set against at least two sourced fear/deprivation passages (confinement dread and money hedging count; the interview habit alone does not), and the article states plainly which way the record leans and how that sets confidence. The money-caution paragraph either moves into this test as fear-center evidence or explains why it does not belong there. The Five sentence is corrected.

findings.passage: His own words point mostly to the second, and the reason starts with that Monday.
findings.problem: His own words split by era, and the article never says so. Nearly every Seven-specific line comes from post-rebrand press, from a creator whose stated method was to 'become that new identity' quickly: the fun rule (April 2025, host-prompted), 'novel ideas' and 'entertaining Kareem' (March 2025), 'talent has a very fun job' (March 2025), 'Something to entertain myself' (2026) and 'the person I'm trying to entertain' (2026). His own account of life before about 28 runs the other way: 'I certainly wasn't following my dreams and my desires... So I just focused on working' and 'It wasn't until honestly, I was like 28 that I started to like really have an opinion and a taste' (S07, both omitted), plus the draft's own 'Interests, likes, none of that was part of the equation.' Years of suppressing desire to fit in are hard for a Seven read to absorb. The Three read, by contrast, predicts a fun-first voice after a deliberate rebrand into an industry that rewards one. The draft concedes that incentive ('Creators are rewarded for saying they do it for fun') but answers it only with present-day costs (see enneagram-05). The opened record does hold unused pre-pivot Seven evidence. Describing in 2023 his move from Vice to The New York Times, he said: 'it's all about juxtaposition and high and low and experiencing all of the things that I can experience. So I really threw myself into that' (Brooklyn Magazine).
findings.acceptance_test: The article names the timing problem plainly: the Seven evidence clusters after the 2019-2020 pivot, and his account of the years before 28 is adaptation and suppressed desire. It then either cites pre-pivot Seven-shaped choices from the record (such as the Vice-to-Times line or the money-for-skiing answer, labeled as 2023 retrospection) or concedes that the pre-pivot record leans Three and adjusts confidence. 'His own words point mostly to the second' is qualified to match.

findings.passage: What gives the line weight is what it costs him. Keep the Meter Running is the clearest case.
findings.problem: The costs answer the 'polish' objection but not the Three alternative, because this is not a choice where fun and recognition pulled apart. Keep the Meter Running is the show whose 2022 press, including Vanity Fair's Bourdain comparison, gave him 'the first time in my life that I felt validated and recognized as a comedian' and left him 'really whole'. The article quotes both lines in the Three section, and in that Forbes answer he also says 'I felt like I made it'. In the same answer he ranks the rewards: 'in terms of validation... the press is still more important. The money is great' (S08, about 00:45:36, omitted). A money-losing show that buys the press he values most is consistent with Three. So the article's strongest costly-choice evidence for the fun rule is recognition-positive. Its own forward test ('If he starts choosing recognition over fun when the two split') implies no split has been observed yet, which sits awkwardly beside 'Three things tip it.'
findings.acceptance_test: The section either (a) cites a sourced, dated choice in which fun and recognition actually diverged and he chose fun (a recognition-neutral or recognition-negative choice); or (b) states plainly that Keep the Meter Running served both his fun and his recognition, so its losses do not separate Seven from Three, and that no clean split has been observed yet. 'Why not Type 3?' then reflects that the decisive split is still prospective.

findings.passage: I am addicted to momentum. I used to tell my therapist that the best part of traveling was the airplane ride. I have a habit of arriving somewhere and then looking forward to going home.
findings.problem: The title ('Addicted to Momentum'), the persona title and the opening present this as a Seven's love of motion, and 'the payoff he names is the ride, not the arrival' leans on it as a discriminator. The newsletter sentences just before it, which the draft drops, set the context as work: 'I don't know how long I can keep up this pace. I probably need to take a break soon, but I don't know how to take breaks because I love work. I am addicted to momentum.' (Another New Thing, September 18, 2024; confirmed on the live page). Being unable to stop working is standard Three material, so the trimmed quote passes shared ground off as Seven-specific. The airplane-ride and arrive-then-leave lines still lean Seven, as does the closing transit quote, but the 'momentum' here is work momentum. The same record also has 'I felt like I made it' (S08) and 'I finally have arrived' (S20), which the article raises only in 'What the type leaves out.'
findings.acceptance_test: Wherever the quote appears, it includes or paraphrases 'I don't know how to take breaks because I love work.' 'Why not Type 3?' says the work-momentum half fits both types and only the anticipation-over-arrival half (the airplane ride, 'more comfortable being in transit') leans Seven. The title and persona title stay only if the editor judges they still fit the corrected framing.

findings.passage: The chameleon story could also suggest Type 9. Nines blend in to keep the peace, though, and Rahma's favorite evening is a four-hour argument.
findings.problem: The quick dismissals rest on behavioral stereotypes, not motive. A debate he says is about 'something that I don't care about' is low-stakes play that a Nine can enjoy, and his own account of the chameleon years ('I didn't want to say anything weird, do anything weird... I certainly wasn't following my dreams and my desires', S07) is Nine-shaped self-forgetting that the dinner table does not rebut. 'An Eight argues to win' is the same kind of stereotype, since Eights also argue for the intensity. The Six, defined in the triad paragraph, is never tested, though the article itself supplies Six-shaped material: safety nets ('I became my own rich parent'; 'If it doesn't work out, I can always sell this stuff') and nearly skipping SubwayTakes until his wife encouraged him.
findings.acceptance_test: Nine, Eight and Six each get one sourced, motive-level reason they trail, or the dismissals are cut. Possible reasons: for Nine, his sustained self-promotion and initiative (the five-year plan, the rebrand); for Eight, his open, repeated statement that he needs validation; for Six, why the hedges are not the organizing motive. No dismissal rests on 'Nines avoid conflict' or 'Eights argue to win.'

findings.passage: That explains a lot about how he works, but not why he names fun as his rule, or why he went back to school the Monday after a funeral.
findings.problem: This dismisses, without support, the main confound for the Seven read's most specific evidence. Interest- and novelty-driven motivation, restlessness and trouble stopping are commonly described features of adult ADHD. So ADHD plausibly bears on 'number one is fun', the novelty language and 'addicted to momentum', not only on how he switches tasks. The same move recurs at 'That half second is the Seven's reframe in miniature'. On a shoot where the driver picks the destination, turning a dull pick into a bit is the host's job and an improv habit. The research record notes his UCB training and lists this alternative; the draft omits it.
findings.acceptance_test: The ADHD paragraph stops asserting that ADHD cannot explain the fun rule. It states the overlap honestly and names what the Seven read adds that ADHD does not (for example his stated reasons for wanting money and fame, and his preference for anticipation over arrival), keeping 'The type describes a pattern of motives, not a diagnosis or a cause.' The Buffalo Wild Wings line is qualified to acknowledge the host and improv explanation.

protected_passages.passage: That is about as Three as a sentence gets, and it is the main reason this read stays at medium confidence.
protected_passages.reason: Confronts the strongest counterevidence in plain words instead of absorbing it with a wing or a caveat. Keep it next to the validation quotes.

protected_passages.passage: A Seven can crave applause, and the validation quotes are what the Seven read absorbs least comfortably. The test going forward is simple. If he starts choosing recognition over fun when the two split, the case for Three gets stronger.
protected_passages.reason: A falsifiable, observable discriminator, which is exactly the right shape. It should frame the Three section rather than close it.

protected_passages.passage: The goal looks like a Three's. The reason he gives is a Seven's.
protected_passages.reason: This is the one discriminator that survives source checking (S08 'talent has a very fun job... You get to do new things'; S05 money so he need not 'say no to fun'). It should carry the argument once the shared-ground reasons are relabeled.

protected_passages.passage: That could be one good quote handed to him by a friendly host. It keeps coming back in other rooms, though.
protected_passages.reason: Model handling of a prompted self-report: it names the prompt, then tests the line for repetition across outlets and years.

protected_passages.passage: I'm not in a hurry to go to the next spot, which may be the first time in my life. I always felt more comfortable being in transit, not literally, but also literally.
protected_passages.reason: The most Seven-specific line in the piece, in its source context (Rolling Stone, 2025). The article also ends on a stated change that the type does not neatly own.

assessment: Type 7 at medium confidence is defensible, but the article argues it with more discriminating force than the record supports. Of the reasons given, two discriminate: what he says the Three's currencies are for (Forbes 2025, 'talent has a very fun job'; Brooklyn Magazine 2023, money so he need not 'say no to fun') and anticipation over arrival (the airplane ride, 'more comfortable being in transit'). The grief motion, the failure narration and Keep the Meter Running's losses are shared with Three. Two quotes are trimmed of their Three-facing context ('one up yourself or don't stop... that's how I coped'; 'I don't know how to take breaks because I love work'). The center test the article itself sets up (fear versus shame) is never run, and the Seven evidence clusters in post-rebrand press, while his own account of life before 28 is adaptation and suppressed desire. The opened sources hold omitted Three evidence ('become that new identity', 'go down in New York history as a legend', 'The headline says you're a comedian... Personally, I do', 'the press is still more important', 'I can't deal with another failure') and omitted Seven evidence ('experiencing all of the things that I can experience', 'underprepared intentionally because I do like the spontaneity'). Credit: Type 3 gets a real section built on its best evidence, the prompted fun quote is labeled, no wing or arrow is used to absorb contradictions, and the forward test is falsifiable. If enneagram-01 to -05 cannot be met, the honest options are to keep Seven with confidence lowered to an explicit 'leans' and the decisive split named as prospective, or to hold for research (independent testimony from Kuo or his wife, or an observed fun-versus-recognition split). Changing the type would require --refresh --expanded-review. Similarity: the tripped pair is the stock connective 'The pattern runs in a few plain steps' (also verbatim in the shyam-sankar draft) against Tyla's 'The pattern runs across four unrelated domains'. The arguments differ, and the mechanism paragraph is tied immediately to his regret quote, so it is not reported as reuse. Method: context was checked in the research-stage saved texts at the cited locators (Brooklyn Magazine transcript, Forbes auto-captions, Death, Sex & Money machine transcript, Interview, Rolling Stone, newsletter). The S12 newsletter and Brooklyn Magazine pages were re-fetched live. No audio was re-listened, so Forbes and Death, Sex & Money wording is machine text, and Forbes speaker attribution rests on continuity.
